title: How monetization works on social media apps
html:
On DeHub, anyone can monetize from their first view, using permissionless smart contracts for subscriptions, PPVs or paid messages. There are no thresholds or requirements, and everything is peer to peer with minor platform fees. All profit is shared between stakeholders too!

Every major social platform now runs some version of a creator revenue program. The labels sound similar (rewards, partnerships, subscriptions, gifts) but the rules behind them are not. One platform pays on watch time. Another pays on verified impressions. A third pays on product sales. A fourth pays only if it invites you first.

Most programs still require a minimum audience and a minimum level of recent activity. Some let you apply the moment you hit those numbers. Others stay invitation-only even after you qualify. TikTok and Instagram give creators several ways to earn from the same account: affiliate tags, fan tips, subscriptions, brand marketplaces, and, in some markets, performance bonuses. Payout minimums and schedules also differ: $5 twice a month on Meta in the U.S., $30 every two weeks on X, $100 with daily cash-out on Snap, $50 on a Net-15 cycle on Twitch.

That fragmentation is why monetization still feels confusing. The thresholds also move. YouTube is doubling its Partner Program entry bar in February 2027. X is replacing Creator Revenue Sharing with Original Content Rewards on September 7, 2026. Meta keeps testing a unified payout model across Reels, videos, photos, and text. A creator who checked the rules six months ago can be working from outdated numbers.

Below is a platform-by-platform breakdown of the current monetization rules for Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, X, Snap, and Twitch, including who can apply, what actually pays, and where the real money usually comes from once the native program is unlocked.

Instagram

  • Minimum audience threshold: About 500 followers for Gifts on Reels; about 1,000 followers for Creator Marketplace and Instagram Affiliate (product tags in posts and Reels); about 10,000 followers for Subscriptions and Live badges.
  • Minimum activity threshold: No public, program-wide posting quota. Bonus programs informally favor creators who post Reels several times a week.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older; Creator or Business account; compliance with Community Guidelines and Partner Monetization Policies.
  • Country/region restrictions: Feature availability varies by market. Subscriptions require an approved-country list. Performance bonuses have historically been concentrated in the U.S., Japan, and South Korea.
  • Invitation status: Gifts, Affiliate, Marketplace, Subscriptions, and Live badges are generally self-serve once eligibility appears in the Professional Dashboard. Bonuses and Meta's tested unified monetization model remain invitation-only.
  • Payout terms: U.S. minimum is typically $5, paid twice a month. Outside the U.S., the floor is often $100 for wire transfer and $25 for other methods.

Instagram does not run one open, per-view creator fund. It runs a stack of separate products. Gifts are the lowest door: viewers send Stars on Reels, and those convert to cash. Subscriptions are the most predictable native product (fans pay a monthly fee for exclusive posts, Reels, Lives, and broadcast-channel access) but they only work if a niche audience will pay to stay close. Live badges function like livestream tipping. Affiliate and Marketplace sit closer to commerce: tag products, take a cut, or get matched with brands. Bonuses are the closest thing Instagram has to a view-based paycheck, and they are the least reliable because Meta chooses the roster, sets the formula, and can pause the program.

That structure shapes how serious Instagram businesses actually get paid. Native tools can add a layer of income, especially subscriptions in a tight niche or a viral Reel that attracts gifts. The larger checks still tend to come from brand deals, UGC, affiliate catalogs, and owned products sold through the bio. Meta has tested a unified model that would treat Reels, videos, photos, and text as one monetization surface, but that test remains invite-only. Instagram and Facebook share a parent company and a payout rail. They do not share the same audience behavior or the same path to money.

TikTok

  • Minimum audience threshold: No follower minimum to sell through your own TikTok Shop if you have an official seller account; about 1,000 followers for LIVE gifts, LIVE subscriptions, and Shop Affiliate entry; 10,000 followers for the Creator Rewards Program, TikTok One / creator marketplace access, and some paywalled Series content; 100,000 followers for premium ad placements such as TikTok Pulse.
  • Minimum activity threshold: Creator Rewards currently requires 100,000 video views in the last 30 days, plus an account in good standing. Series generally needs recent public posting. Pulse is reserved for top-performing, high-engagement inventory.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older (19 in South Korea); Personal account for Creator Rewards; compliance with Community Guidelines and the Creator Code of Conduct. Business accounts are typically excluded from Rewards.
  • Country/region restrictions: Creator Rewards is limited to a short list of markets, commonly including the U.S., U.K., Germany, France, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, and Brazil. Large parts of the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Africa, Canada, and Australia do not have Rewards. TikTok remains banned in India and several sanctioned countries.
  • Invitation status: Most programs are open once thresholds are met. Pulse and paid marketplace campaigns are offer-driven: you can join a directory, but you earn when a brand or the platform books you.
  • Payout terms: Country-dependent. In the U.S., a $10 monthly minimum is common.

TikTok's fork in the road is still the most important decision on the platform. One path is commerce: Shop, affiliate links, LIVE selling, and custom commission rates. The other is media: original videos long enough to qualify for Creator Rewards, usually a minute or more, paid on qualified views rather than raw views. Affiliate has the lower barrier. Brand deals and Pulse inventory can pay more per placement. Rewards sits in the middle, scalable if the algorithm keeps delivering qualified views, fragile if watch time or originality drops.

The economics are uneven on purpose. TikTok Shop's U.S. platform commission is commonly cited around 9% per item sold, while affiliates negotiate their own cut. Creator-reported Rewards ranges in 2026 often land somewhere between a few hundred dollars and a little over $1,000 per million qualified views, depending on country, content type, and how much of the view TikTok counts as qualified. That is why two accounts with similar follower counts can report wildly different months. Marketers still treat TikTok as the first short-form bet: recent benchmark surveys have put it well ahead of Instagram for new creator-platform investment.

YouTube

  • Minimum audience threshold: 500 subscribers for fan funding (Super Chat, Super Thanks, channel memberships) and YouTube Shopping tools; 1,000 subscribers for ads and Premium revenue sharing.
  • Minimum activity threshold: Fan funding currently requires three public uploads in the last 90 days plus 3,000 watch hours in the last year or 3 million public Shorts views in the last 90 days. Ads and Premium currently require 4,000 watch hours in the last year or 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older, or a parent/guardian setup; two-step verification; an active AdSense account; compliance with YouTube's policies and advertiser-friendly guidelines.
  • Country/region restrictions: Monetization is available in more than 120 countries. Google suspended ad services in Russia in 2022. The platform is blocked in countries such as China, Iran, and North Korea.
  • Invitation status: Open application through YouTube Studio once thresholds are met.
  • Payout terms: $100 minimum (or local equivalent), paid monthly, with unpaid balances rolling forward.

YouTube remains the closest thing the creator economy has to a long-term salary machine, and it is tightening the front door. From February 1, 2027, new applicants for ads and Premium revenue sharing will need 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 qualified watch hours in the previous 365 days, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the previous 90 days. Existing Partner Program members keep long-form monetization even if they are below those new entry numbers. They do have to accept updated Studio terms by January 31, 2027.

The more immediate change is the Shorts floor. Starting February 1, 2027, a channel needs 10 million qualified Shorts views in the trailing 90 days to earn from the Shorts Creator Pool that month. Fall below it and you are not kicked out of YPP. You simply stop earning on Shorts until the rolling window recovers. Long-form ads keep paying. YouTube is also adding a clearer "active channel" test: 1,000 qualified watch hours in 365 days, 1 million Shorts views in 90 days, or a minimum upload cadence of two long-form videos or five Shorts every 90 days.

The revenue split still favors long-form. Industry tracking commonly puts YouTube's take at about 45% of long-form ad revenue, with creators keeping the rest, while fan-funded products such as Super Chat are often closer to a 30% platform cut. Shorts pay from a shared pool and, for most channels, remain the weaker dollar-per-view product. That is why the 2027 changes matter: YouTube is no longer trying to get every new Shorts account into the ad pool as quickly as possible. It is trying to reserve ads and Premium sharing for channels that can sustain attention.

Facebook

  • Minimum audience threshold: About 500 followers for at least 30 consecutive days for Stars; about 10,000 followers for Subscriptions; no public follower minimum for affiliate tools; no fully public threshold for Content Monetization because that program is invite-only.
  • Minimum activity threshold: Subscriptions commonly require 50,000 post engagements or 180,000 watch minutes in the last 60 days. Content Monetization uses internal quality and performance screens rather than a single published number.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older (or parental permission where allowed); professional or personal account at least 20 days old; original, authentic content; compliance with Community Standards and monetization policies.
  • Country/region restrictions: Monetization products are available in roughly 70 countries, with each tool rolling out on its own map.
  • Invitation status: Content Monetization is invite-only, though creators can express interest in the Professional Dashboard. Stars, affiliate, and some subscription features are more open. Creator Fast Track is a separate on-ramp for creators with audiences on other platforms.
  • Payout terms: U.S. minimum is typically $5. Outside the U.S., $100 for wire transfer and $25 for other methods is common. Payouts are often released around the 21st of each month.

Facebook is trying to solve a credibility problem and a discovery problem at the same time. The credibility problem is content quality: it is one of the few major platforms that openly says monetization can be pulled for misinformation, clickbait, sensationalism, and false news. The discovery problem is that many working creators built their audience on TikTok, Instagram, or YouTube and never treated Facebook as a home base.

Creator Fast Track is Meta's answer to that second problem. Eligible creators with established followings elsewhere can get boosted Reels distribution and a short window of guaranteed pay (commonly $1,000 a month at 100,000-plus followers on Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube, and $3,000 a month at 1 million-plus) in exchange for posting a set number of eligible Reels. After the guarantee period, those accounts are supposed to roll into regular Content Monetization. Meta also launched a standalone, AI-powered Creator Studio app that recommends edits, pacing, and voiceover changes. Creator Ronica Rupan told Digiday that the first Reel she adjusted from those suggestions performed 86% better than her previous average.

The legal backdrop still hangs over the product. In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement over child-safety claims and said it would add more teen time limits and restricted features on Instagram and Facebook. Adult monetization itself should be unaffected (you generally must be 18 to get paid) but teen-usage limits can change the overall attention pool that ads and recommendations compete for.

X

  • Minimum audience threshold: 500 verified followers.
  • Minimum activity threshold: For Original Content Rewards, 500,000 Home Timeline impressions from verified users in the last 90 days, with reply impressions excluded. Creators must also post original content on a regular basis.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older; Personal or Business account; active X Premium, Premium+, or Premium Business subscription; compliance with the X User Agreement and monetization standards. Premium Basic does not qualify.
  • Country/region restrictions: Available in more than 110 countries, with the official help-center list as the source of truth.
  • Invitation status: Application through Creator Studio once eligibility appears. New enrollments into the old Revenue Sharing program are closed.
  • Payout terms: $30 minimum, paid every two weeks, typically via Stripe or X Money after identity verification.

On September 7, 2026, X shuts down earnings under Creator Revenue Sharing. On September 8, existing members can start applying to the replacement: Original Content Rewards. The old program paid against a much larger impression pile, 5 million organic impressions in three months, and became associated with reply-bait, aggregated clips, and accounts optimized for ad load rather than authorship. The new program lowers the raw impression number and raises the quality test.

What counts now is a qualified Home Timeline impression: a unique view of an original post, from a verified or Premium user, with a substantial portion of the post on screen. Repeat views from the same account, paid distribution, and fraudulent impressions are out. So is content that is copied, lightly cropped, or re-uploaded from another account without "meaningful original value." X's creator-product lead, Allegra Jacchia, told Digiday the old revenue-share model had "run its course" and that the new program is meant to signal support for high-quality creators whether they are small, new, or already large.

The catch is structural. Creators still have to pay for a Premium tier to earn from the platform. That makes X the rare major network where the ticket into the payout program is itself a subscription. For writers, reporters, analysts, and operators who already publish native posts, the new math can be cleaner than the old reply-ad model. For accounts built on other people's media, the program is a warning.

Snap

  • Minimum audience threshold: 50,000 followers for the unified Monetization Program.
  • Minimum activity threshold: Snap's current public bar is 15,000 hours of view time in the last 28 days, including at least 3,000 hours from Spotlight. Since May 7, 2026, creators also need at least 100 hours of Spotlight view time in the trailing 28 days to qualify for maximum rewards. Spotlight videos generally need to be long enough to carry ads, commonly around one minute. Regular posting (often cited as 25 times a month or activity on 10 of the last 28 days) remains part of the Snap Star / monetization profile.
  • Account requirements: Verified Snap Star; 18 or the age of majority; original, advertiser-friendly, authentic content; compliance with Community Guidelines and monetization terms.
  • Country/region restrictions: Eligibility varies by monetization surface, including Story mid-roll ads, Spotlight rewards, and Lens Creator Rewards.
  • Invitation status: Snap Star is an application. Monetization is an invitation. Hitting the numbers makes you eligible for review, not automatically paid.
  • Payout terms: $100 minimum, with daily cash-out once payout onboarding is complete.

Snap is easy to underestimate because it does not behave like a public follower graph. Its creator economy is split between people who post Stories and Spotlight videos and people who build AR Lenses. Lens Creator Rewards pay developers when other Snapchatters use their filters; a Lens that reaches a high number of qualified posters in its first 90 days can trigger a top-performer payout. For conventional creators, the money is an ad share on public Stories and eligible Spotlight inventory.

That second path can be surprisingly lucrative for the small set of accounts that live inside Snap's recommendation loop. One creator told Digiday they rarely make less than $200 a day on the platform. Another, Abby Berner, said Snap out-earned her other channels in 2025, more than $500,000, even though her TikTok audience was much larger. The tradeoff is the invitation wall and the watch-time treadmill. Followers alone do not get you paid. The 28-day hour count does.

Twitch

  • Minimum audience threshold: Affiliate: 25 followers, plus an average of about 3 concurrent viewers on four different days. Partner: an average of 75 viewers across qualifying streams in two consecutive months, commonly six streams at 75 average viewers in each of two months.
  • Minimum activity threshold: Affiliate now requires 4 hours streamed on 4 different days inside a rolling 30-day window, along with the viewer and follower floors. Partner remains a high-consistency test plus a manual review.
  • Account requirements: 18 or older, or 13-plus with parental permission; two-factor authentication; content that follows Community Guidelines.
  • Country/region restrictions: Affiliate is broadly global, with exceptions tied to tax rules, network fees, or sanctions. Kenya and South Korea have been among the restricted or special-case markets.
  • Invitation status: Affiliate invites are issued automatically after the four conditions overlap. Partner is an application after the viewer bar is cleared.
  • Payout terms: $50 minimum for most methods, $100 for wire transfer, paid about 15 days after the month closes (Net 15).

Twitch changed the shape of its ladder in 2026. Monetization for All, rolled out globally in May, lets eligible streamers turn on subscriptions, Bits, emotes, badges, and Channel Points before they are Affiliates. They can collect a balance. They cannot cash it out until they become an Affiliate or Partner. In the meantime, some markets offer a Spendable Balance that can be used inside Twitch, for example on Bits or gifted subs.

The Affiliate bar also dropped. The old mix of 50 followers, 8 hours, and 7 streaming days is gone. The current test is designed for people who cannot broadcast every night: 25 followers, 4 hours, 4 days, and a small concurrent-viewer floor. "Our approach to monetization is simple," Twitch chief product officer Mike Minton said. "Give creators more ways to earn earlier in their journey and as they grow. We don't think a creator needs a massive audience to have built something valuable."

The payout split still rewards scale. The default subscription split is 50/50. Eligible streamers can move to 60/40 or 70/30 as paid-sub performance rises. Partner adds ad inventory, better transcoding, longer VOD storage, and a clearer brand-deal path; Affiliates recently gained access to Twitch's sponsorship portal as well. The unsolved problem is discovery. The home page still surfaces high-CCV live channels, which means a new streamer can now collect subs in theory and still struggle to get the viewers who make those subs add up.

The practical takeaway

The platforms are no longer asking the same question. Instagram asks whether fans will pay or brands will buy. TikTok asks whether you can sell a product or hold a qualified view. YouTube asks whether you can hold attention for a year at a time. Facebook asks whether it trusts your content enough to put ads around it. X asks whether the post is yours. Snap asks whether people will keep watching for hours, not seconds. Twitch asks whether a small room of people will come back live.

That is why "getting monetized" is no longer one milestone. It is a stack of product-specific gates, and the smartest creators treat the native payout as one line in a spreadsheet rather than the business itself. The rules above are the current map. Check the in-app dashboard before you build a year of work around any single number. These programs change faster than the pages that explain them.

The catch is structural. Creators still have to pay for a Premium tier to earn from the platform. That makes X the rare major network where the ticket into the payout program is itself a subscription. For writers, reporters, analysts, and operators who already publish native posts, the new math can be cleaner than the old reply-ad model. For accounts built on other people's media, the program is a warning.

## Snap

![Snap pays on a rolling 28-day watch-hour count, not on follower count](/lovable-uploads/fig-monetization-snap.jpg)

- **Minimum audience threshold:** 50,000 followers for the unified Monetization Program.
- **Minimum activity threshold:** Snap's current public bar is 15,000 hours of view time in the last 28 days, including at least 3,000 hours from Spotlight. Since May 7, 2026, creators also need at least 100 hours of Spotlight view time in the trailing 28 days to qualify for maximum rewards. Spotlight videos generally need to be long enough to carry ads, commonly around one minute. Regular posting (often cited as 25 times a month or activity on 10 of the last 28 days) remains part of the Snap Star / monetization profile.
- **Account requirements:** Verified Snap Star; 18 or the age of majority; original, advertiser-friendly, authentic content; compliance with Community Guidelines and monetization terms.
- **Country/region restrictions:** Eligibility varies by monetization surface, including Story mid-roll ads, Spotlight rewards, and Lens Creator Rewards.
- **Invitation status:** Snap Star is an application. Monetization is an invitation. Hitting the numbers makes you eligible for review, not automatically paid.
- **Payout terms:** $100 minimum, with daily cash-out once payout onboarding is complete.

Snap is easy to underestimate because it does not behave like a public follower graph. Its creator economy is split between people who post Stories and Spotlight videos and people who build AR Lenses. Lens Creator Rewards pay developers when other Snapchatters use their filters; a Lens that reaches a high number of qualified posters in its first 90 days can trigger a top-performer payout. For conventional creators, the money is an ad share on public Stories and eligible Spotlight inventory.

That second path can be surprisingly lucrative for the small set of accounts that live inside Snap's recommendation loop. One creator told Digiday they rarely make less than $200 a day on the platform. Another, Abby Berner, said Snap out-earned her other channels in 2025, more than $500,000, even though her TikTok audience was much larger. The tradeoff is the invitation wall and the watch-time treadmill. Followers alone do not get you paid. The 28-day hour count does.

## Twitch

![Twitch now lets streamers switch on subscriptions and Bits before they are Affiliates](/lovable-uploads/fig-monetization-twitch.jpg)

- **Minimum audience threshold:** Affiliate: 25 followers, plus an average of about 3 concurrent viewers on four different days. Partner: an average of 75 viewers across qualifying streams in two consecutive months, commonly six streams at 75 average viewers in each of two months.
- **Minimum activity threshold:** Affiliate now requires 4 hours streamed on 4 different days inside a rolling 30-day window, along with the viewer and follower floors. Partner remains a high-consistency test plus a manual review.
- **Account requirements:** 18 or older, or 13-plus with parental permission; two-factor authentication; content that follows Community Guidelines.
- **Country/region restrictions:** Affiliate is broadly global, with exceptions tied to tax rules, network fees, or sanctions. Kenya and South Korea have been among the restricted or special-case markets.
- **Invitation status:** Affiliate invites are issued automatically after the four conditions overlap. Partner is an application after the viewer bar is cleared.
- **Payout terms:** $50 minimum for most methods, $100 for wire transfer, paid about 15 days after the month closes (Net 15).

Twitch changed the shape of its ladder in 2026. Monetization for All, rolled out globally in May, lets eligible streamers turn on subscriptions, Bits, emotes, badges, and Channel Points before they are Affiliates. They can collect a balance. They cannot cash it out until they become an Affiliate or Partner. In the meantime, some markets offer a Spendable Balance that can be used inside Twitch, for example on Bits or gifted subs.

The Affiliate bar also dropped. The old mix of 50 followers, 8 hours, and 7 streaming days is gone. The current test is designed for people who cannot broadcast every night: 25 followers, 4 hours, 4 days, and a small concurrent-viewer floor. "Our approach to monetization is simple," Twitch chief product officer Mike Minton said. "Give creators more ways to earn earlier in their journey and as they grow. We don't think a creator needs a massive audience to have built something valuable."

The payout split still rewards scale. The default subscription split is 50/50. Eligible streamers can move to 60/40 or 70/30 as paid-sub performance rises. Partner adds ad inventory, better transcoding, longer VOD storage, and a clearer brand-deal path; Affiliates recently gained access to Twitch's sponsorship portal as well. The unsolved problem is discovery. The home page still surfaces high-CCV live channels, which means a new streamer can now collect subs in theory and still struggle to get the viewers who make those subs add up.

## The practical takeaway

The platforms are no longer asking the same question. Instagram asks whether fans will pay or brands will buy. TikTok asks whether you can sell a product or hold a qualified view. YouTube asks whether you can hold attention for a year at a time. Facebook asks whether it trusts your content enough to put ads around it. X asks whether the post is yours. Snap asks whether people will keep watching for hours, not seconds. Twitch asks whether a small room of people will come back live.

That is why "getting monetized" is no longer one milestone. It is a stack of product-specific gates, and the smartest creators treat the native payout as one line in a spreadsheet rather than the business itself. The rules above are the current map. Check the in-app dashboard before you build a year of work around any single number. These programs change faster than the pages that explain them.
